subject: Mixture of a truncated and unconstrained normal distribution.

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Mixture of a truncated and unconstrained normal distribution.
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to set up a regression model in Stan in which the outcome variable is a mixture of an unconstrained normal distribution and a truncated normal distribution.

Unfortunately, I am already getting stuck in my preliminary attempts to model the mixture of a truncated and an unconstrained distribution.

I’d greatly appreciate any feedback to the following approach:

 

In short:

The key section of the model block implementing the updating for a mixture of a constrained and unconstrained normal distribution is as follows:

(I know that mu and sigma of both groups are identical)

for (n in 1:N) {

      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma);

      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma) - normal_ccdf_log(L, mu, sigma) ;

    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));

  }

This model does not work (slow, low n_eff, bad posterior means), and I unfortunately do not understand why.

 

 

In Detail:

The case-control study consists of a larger group of "cases", i.e. people who have a symptom score above a cutoff, and a smaller group of randomly sampled "control" participants

(Ultimately i will have to use a Poisson model, because symptom scores are integers, but I though I start simple.)


##1## simulate data reflecting the sampling strategy of the study in R, using the truncnorm package:

L = qnorm(.75)

y = c(rnorm(500),rtruncnorm(1000,a = L))

 

##2## put together a list stan_data

stan_data = list(y = y, N = length(y), K = 2, L = L, theta = c(1/3, 2/3))

 

##3## the Stan model implements two things I know about the experiments:

## because the two groups come from the same population, both groups have the same mu and sigma

## I know mixing proportions and that the larger group has truncated y, and include this into the model

## As outlined in the Stan language documentation I use the increment_log_prob function  to update over groups and to implement the truncation.

data {

  int<lower=1> K;      // number of mixture components

  int<lower=1> N;      // number of data points

  real y[N];                // observations

  simplex[K] theta;    // mixing proportions

  real L;                   // cutoff, lower bound for truncated distribution

}

parameters {

  real mu;             // locations of mixture components

  real<lower=0> sigma; // scales of mixture components

}

model {

  real ps[K];             // temp for log component densities

  sigma ~ cauchy(0,1);

  mu ~ normal(0,1);

  for (n in 1:N) {

      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma); // 

      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma) - normal_ccdf_log(L, mu, sigma) ;

    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));

  }

}

 

This seems straight forward to me, and I had expected that this simple case should not be a problem. But when I run this model with 1000 iterations I find it to be very slow and inefficient (e.g. total runtime 2200s, n_eff between 6 and 40) and the posterior means for mu (-11.71) and sigma (1.57) are nowhere near their true values of 0 and 1 I used to generate the data. (Note that I am already using relatively tight priors, initializing with true parameter values did also not help). Given how long it takes to run 1000 iterations, I assume that the solution is not to simply run longer chains.

 

I also tried a model with separate mu and sigma for the two groups (code below). This model is also very slow (e.g. 5676.97 s for 2500 samples) and inefficient (n_eff between 3 and 6).

 

Now I am wondering if I am overlooking something fundamental here, have an undetected bug, or if the estimation this model is just harder than I thought.


 

Any thoughts?

 

Cheers - Guido  

 

 

 

### model with separate mu and sigma for groups

data {

  int<lower=1> K;      // number of mixture components

  int<lower=1> N;      // number of data points

  real y[N];           // observations

  simplex[K] theta;    // mixing proportions

  real L;              // cutoff, lower bound for truncated distribution

}

parameters {

  real mu[K];             // locations of mixture components

  real<lower=0> sigma[K]; // scales of mixture components

}

 

model {

  real ps[K];             // temp for log component densities

  sigma ~ cauchy(0,1);

  mu ~ normal(0,1);

  for (n in 1:N) {

      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(y[n],mu[1],sigma[1]);

      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + normal_log(y[n],mu[2],sigma[2]) - normal_ccdf_log(L, mu[2], sigma[2]) ;

    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));

  }

}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture of a truncated and unconstrained normal distribution.
parts:
Thanks for the careful dump of the problem.

It looks like your'e trying to mix a normal with its own
truncated version with an unknown truncation point L,

* normal(mu,sigma)

* normal(mu,sigma) T[L, ]

The L in your model is unconstrained, but as it's written,
you don't put the probability to zero of the mixture component
with the truncation.

I definitely need to mention this in the manual. See:



Did you check what happened to L? I'm guessing it would go to infinity
in your model, making the CCDF term blow up. That would definitely
kill sampling.

I think what you want is to do this:

if (y[n] < L)
increment_log_prob(log(theta[1]) + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma));
else
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta[1])
+ normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma),

- normal_ccdf_log(L,mu,sigma)));
}

I'm still not sure that'll mix well --- I'd be inclined to plot out
the density as a function of L at the known true values of mu and
sigma just to see what it looks like. I don't think we've done
much with unknown truncation points in models.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture of a truncated and unconstrained normal distribution.
parts:
Thanks for the quick reply Bob!

 

I would hope that L is not the problem in this specific model, because I know L and simply submit it to the model.

I probably should have said that, because this is not the usual case. If you look at the Stan model (in the detailed description), you will see that L is a data point submitted to the model (I could have made that clearer), and that L does not appear in the parameter block.

 

Still, your suggestion to use the value of y to decide how the log probability is incremented solved my problem.

Thanks a lot!

Guido

It looks like your'e trying to mix a normal with its own

The L in your model is unconstrained, but as it's written,
you don't put the probability to zero of the mixture component
with the truncation.

I definitely need to mention this in the manual.  See:



Did you check what happened to L?  I'm guessing it would go to infinity
in your model, making the CCDF term blow up.  That would definitely
kill sampling.

I think what you want is to do this:

 for (n in 1:N) {

   else
     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta[1])
                                      + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma),
                                    log(theta[2])
                                      + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma)
                                      - normal_ccdf_log(L,mu,sigma)));
  }

I'm still not sure that'll mix well --- I'd be inclined to plot out
the density as a function of L at the known true values of mu and
sigma just to see what it looks like.  I don't think we've done
much with unknown truncation points in models.

- Bob
